case_summary.critical_gap_explanation: Operative instruments (N002, N136, N141, N001) supported by N133 require the final submission to be the student's own work, prohibit unapproved or undisclosed GenAI use, and provide authenticity monitoring and appeal remedies.
case_summary.case_note: Curtin prescribes that GenAI use in assessment requires explicit Unit Coordinator permission and transparent disclosure, and that the final submission must be the student's own work (N002, N133, N136, N141). All S1 critical-risk safeguards—attributable authorship, disclosure, human accountability, equity, and appeal remedies—are addressed (D5=3, Critical gap=No), though Unit Coordinator permission criteria and steps remain undocumented (D2=2, D4=2).

case_summary.critical_risk_criterion: Prevention or enforceable refusal of unverified AI-produced assessment being claimed as the student's own.
case_summary.critical_gap_explanation: Under Protocol v1.1, an enforceable prohibition protects the critical risk: Curtin prohibits submitting AI-generated output as one's own work (N136, N133), requires authenticity verification and Confirmation Checks (N002), and enforces penalties under N141.
case_summary.case_note: Curtin prohibits students from submitting AI-drafted work as their own without explicit permission and disclosure, treating unapproved or undisclosed GenAI output as academic misconduct (N136, N133, N141). Operative assessment rules also require staff authenticity verification, Confirmation Checks, and 50% Secure Assessment or monitoring (N002), so S2's critical risk is protected (D5=3, Critical gap=No).

decision made using AI. Maintain records on the use of AI to comply with
recordkeeping obligations.

documents_checked.document_title: Curtin University AI Use in Research
documents_checked.text:
AI tools can enhance research by quickly summarising or refining text, analysing large data sets, crafting and debugging code, communicating research
results and streamlining repetitive tasks. To use them well, researchers need to protect intellectual integrity and authorship, safeguard intellectual
property (including Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property), use data in culturally appropriate ways, and keep human oversight and expert
judgement at the centre of their work. AI tools must never substitute for human critical thinking, expertise and evaluation.
The guidelines apply to all Curtin researchers, including research students in master and doctoral programs. They cover generative AI tools for text,
images, audio, code and data, as well as generative AI-driven support platforms. They should be read alongside Curtin’s Artificial Intelligence Policy and
the policies of publishers, funders and governments relevant to your research.

documents_checked.document_title: Curtin University AI Use in Research
documents_checked.text:
AI tools can enhance research by quickly summarising or refining text, analysing large data sets, crafting and debugging code, communicating research
results and streamlining repetitive tasks. To use them well, researchers need to protect intellectual integrity and authorship, safeguard intellectual
property (including Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property), use data in culturally appropriate ways, and keep human oversight and expert
judgement at the centre of their work. AI tools must never substitute for human critical thinking, expertise and evaluation.
The guidelines apply to all Curtin researchers, including research students in master and doctoral programs. They cover generative AI tools for text,
images, audio, code and data, as well as generative AI-driven support platforms. They should be read alongside Curtin’s Artificial Intelligence Policy and
the policies of publishers, funders and governments relevant to your research.

Substituting AI-simulated responses for approved human participants without ethics authorisation or disclosure is therefore enforceably prohibited (D5=3, Critical gap=No).

documents_checked.text:
AI tools can enhance research by quickly summarising or refining text, analysing large data sets, crafting and debugging code, communicating research
results and streamlining repetitive tasks. To use them well, researchers need to protect intellectual integrity and authorship, safeguard intellectual
property (including Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property), use data in culturally appropriate ways, and keep human oversight and expert
judgement at the centre of their work. AI tools must never substitute for human critical thinking, expertise and evaluation.
The guidelines apply to all Curtin researchers, including research students in master and doctoral programs. They cover generative AI tools for text,
images, audio, code and data, as well as generative AI-driven support platforms. They should be read alongside Curtin’s Artificial Intelligence Policy and
the policies of publishers, funders and governments relevant to your research.

Principle 6: Transparency, Explainability and Contestability
Develop, deploy and use AI systems in a way that maximises transparency,
explainability and contestability. Allow stakeholders to know when AI has
been used and contest decisions made using AI.
Principle 7: Accountability
Implement human oversight, review and the ability to intervene for all AI-
based functions and decisions. Identify the individual accountable for any
decision made using AI. Maintain records on the use of AI to comply with
recordkeeping obligations.

Principle 4: Privacy protection and security
Comply with applicable data protection, security and privacy policies and
legislation. Adhere to the University’s architecture standards if incorporating
AI systems into the University’s enterprise information technology systems.
Principle 5: Reliability and safety
Operate AI systems in accordance with the approved and intended purpose
and monitor their performance. Adopt safety measures proportionate to the
magnitude of potential risks.
Principle 6: Transparency, Explainability and Contestability
Develop, deploy and use AI systems in a way that maximises transparency,
explainability and contestability. Allow stakeholders to know when AI has
been used and contest decisions made using AI.
Principle 7: Accountability
Implement human oversight, review and the ability to intervene for all AI-
based functions and decisions. Identify the individual accountable for any
decision made using AI. Maintain records on the use of AI to comply with
recordkeeping obligations.

evidence.text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is already part of how students learn. Whether we design for it or not, students are using
AI tools to explore ideas, draft responses, and make sense of complex information. When left unguided, however,
students risk using AI in ways that bypass learning or compromise the integrity of their work.
evidence.version_evidence: Written by Dr Megan Ellyard | 02 Jul 2026

evidence.text:
When students use AI repeatedly and authentically in learning tasks, they build their ability to judge when AI is
useful, evaluate what it produces, and experience what it means to remain accountable for the final work. When
coupled with learning and assessment designs that ask students to explain how and why they used AI, and to clarify
their own contribution to AI-augmented work, AI-integrated learning can nurture academic integrity behaviours by
rewarding transparency, honesty and accountability. Making these behaviours more visible also means educators
are positioned to guide students’ decision-making, provide feedback on their AI use, and assess not only what
students produce, but how responsibly they arrived there.

case_summary.critical_risk_criterion: Verified authority for standing account actions, protected student identity and meaningful assessment oversight.
case_summary.critical_gap_explanation: N093 strictly prohibits sharing accounts or concealing identity on University systems, and N090 and N154 enforce student authorship and Student Identity Verification, preventing standing autonomous agent submissions.
case_summary.case_note: ECU prohibits delegating standing account authority to an autonomous AI agent under N093, which restricts University accounts to exclusive personal use and forbids concealing user identity. Submitting coursework without human review also breaches N090 own-work requirements and N154 Student Identity Verification rules.

supporting_passages.text:
This policy applies to:
Complaints made by prospective, current and former Students or members of the public about
the University or University-related conduct, whether occurring in Australia or overseas; and
all persons involved in making, responding to, managing or resolving those Complaints.
Where legislation or another University or external framework provides a specific process for
dealing with all or part of a matter, the University may refer or manage that matter under the
applicable process. This includes matters concerning academic review or appeal, public
interest disclosures, misconduct, staff performance, privacy, employment or workplace
grievances, the ECU Student Guild, and third-party organisations.
This does not prevent the University from considering a distinct Complaint about its
administration of, or response to, the matter.
Where a matter engages more than one framework, the University will determine whether the
relevant issues are to be managed separately, sequentially, concurrently or in a coordinated
manner and will inform the Complainant of the applicable pathway.

review_route_evidence.text:
This policy applies to:
Complaints made by prospective, current and former Students or members of the public about
the University or University-related conduct, whether occurring in Australia or overseas; and
all persons involved in making, responding to, managing or resolving those Complaints.
Where legislation or another University or external framework provides a specific process for
dealing with all or part of a matter, the University may refer or manage that matter under the
applicable process. This includes matters concerning academic review or appeal, public
interest disclosures, misconduct, staff performance, privacy, employment or workplace
grievances, the ECU Student Guild, and third-party organisations.
This does not prevent the University from considering a distinct Complaint about its
administration of, or response to, the matter.
Where a matter engages more than one framework, the University will determine whether the
relevant issues are to be managed separately, sequentially, concurrently or in a coordinated
manner and will inform the Complainant of the applicable pathway.

The quality and extent of participation in learning and teaching activities may be a component
of assessment. Where participation is used for assessment, explicit marking criteria must be
identified and used, and a record must be kept by the Staff member conducting the class. The
participation component of a final grade will not normally exceed 10 percent of the total
marks.
While attendance at all scheduled learning activities is strongly encouraged and considered
essential for Student success, attendance may not be a component of grades for Students, i.e.
marks cannot be awarded for attendance alone. Attendance may be mandatory (required for
Unit completion) under certain circumstances. Reasons for mandatory attendance may
include:
statutory issues such as mandatory occupational health and safety training;
professional accreditation requirements; or
that a Student’s absence would have a significant effect on other Students’ studies.

documents_checked.text:
When students use AI repeatedly and authentically in learning tasks, they build their ability to judge when AI is
useful, evaluate what it produces, and experience what it means to remain accountable for the final work. When
coupled with learning and assessment designs that ask students to explain how and why they used AI, and to clarify
their own contribution to AI-augmented work, AI-integrated learning can nurture academic integrity behaviours by
rewarding transparency, honesty and accountability. Making these behaviours more visible also means educators
are positioned to guide students’ decision-making, provide feedback on their AI use, and assess not only what
students produce, but how responsibly they arrived there.

supporting_passages.text:
This policy applies to:
Complaints made by prospective, current and former Students or members of the public about
the University or University-related conduct, whether occurring in Australia or overseas; and
all persons involved in making, responding to, managing or resolving those Complaints.
Where legislation or another University or external framework provides a specific process for
dealing with all or part of a matter, the University may refer or manage that matter under the
applicable process. This includes matters concerning academic review or appeal, public
interest disclosures, misconduct, staff performance, privacy, employment or workplace
grievances, the ECU Student Guild, and third-party organisations.
This does not prevent the University from considering a distinct Complaint about its
administration of, or response to, the matter.
Where a matter engages more than one framework, the University will determine whether the
relevant issues are to be managed separately, sequentially, concurrently or in a coordinated
manner and will inform the Complainant of the applicable pathway.

documents_checked.text:
When students use AI repeatedly and authentically in learning tasks, they build their ability to judge when AI is
useful, evaluate what it produces, and experience what it means to remain accountable for the final work. When
coupled with learning and assessment designs that ask students to explain how and why they used AI, and to clarify
their own contribution to AI-augmented work, AI-integrated learning can nurture academic integrity behaviours by
rewarding transparency, honesty and accountability. Making these behaviours more visible also means educators
are positioned to guide students’ decision-making, provide feedback on their AI use, and assess not only what
students produce, but how responsibly they arrived there.

documents_checked.text:
Assessment Panels
Each School must have an Assessment Panel comprising Teaching Staff from the Course Stage,
and other Staff as determined by the Executive Dean of the School (e.g. Course Coordinator)
and have oversight by the Associate Dean (Teaching and Learning). The Assessment Panel will
have sufficient subject matter expertise relevant to the Course.
Where Student performance is assessed across different locations, Schools, providers or
Courses, the Course Coordinator(s) must be included in the Assessment Panel.
The Assessment Panel is to holistically evaluate a combined selection of evidence in order to
confirm a Student’s progression and completion with reference to the CLOs.
The Assessment Panel may conduct an informal viva with a Student where they deem it
necessary for Student Identity Verification or to verify CLO progress and achievement.
The Assessment Panel will provide each Student with feedback on Assessments, describing
their progression towards achievement of the CLOs and providing advice about how to best
approach their learning throughout the remainder of their Course.
Consistent with a criterion and standards referenced approach, where grades are provided, the
allocation of a grade must reflect the level of Student attainment in relation to Benchmarked
Standards. Any scaling of marks must be justifiable by reference to Benchmarked Standards
and endorsed by the Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Education).
Consensus moderation must be employed by Assessment Panels to ensure reliable judgements
in relation to Benchmarked Standards during all phases of the Assessment cycle.

This policy applies to:
Complaints made by prospective, current and former Students or members of the public about
the University or University-related conduct, whether occurring in Australia or overseas; and
all persons involved in making, responding to, managing or resolving those Complaints.
Where legislation or another University or external framework provides a specific process for
dealing with all or part of a matter, the University may refer or manage that matter under the
applicable process. This includes matters concerning academic review or appeal, public
interest disclosures, misconduct, staff performance, privacy, employment or workplace
grievances, the ECU Student Guild, and third-party organisations.
This does not prevent the University from considering a distinct Complaint about its
administration of, or response to, the matter.
Where a matter engages more than one framework, the University will determine whether the
relevant issues are to be managed separately, sequentially, concurrently or in a coordinated
manner and will inform the Complainant of the applicable pathway.

Feedback on Student work may be generated through self and peer review and assessment so
that Students have an opportunity to practise applying criteria and standards to their own
work and that of others. The following must be met:
peer review and peer assessment processes must be designed to ensure that Students can be
treated with respect by other Students, and must be supported by clear guidelines and criteria
for the review;
Students must always receive Feedback on their self and peer reviews and assessments to
assist them in calibrating their judgement to match discipline standards;
Self and peer assessment is to be used for Formative Assessment purposes only – the grading
of Student work is the Unit Coordinator’s responsibility; and
if Students are required to generate constructive Feedback for a peer, the quality of such
Feedback may be a component of Summative Assessment.

documents_checked.text:
Assessment Panels
Each School must have an Assessment Panel comprising Teaching Staff from the Course Stage,
and other Staff as determined by the Executive Dean of the School (e.g. Course Coordinator)
and have oversight by the Associate Dean (Teaching and Learning). The Assessment Panel will
have sufficient subject matter expertise relevant to the Course.
Where Student performance is assessed across different locations, Schools, providers or
Courses, the Course Coordinator(s) must be included in the Assessment Panel.
The Assessment Panel is to holistically evaluate a combined selection of evidence in order to
confirm a Student’s progression and completion with reference to the CLOs.
The Assessment Panel may conduct an informal viva with a Student where they deem it
necessary for Student Identity Verification or to verify CLO progress and achievement.
The Assessment Panel will provide each Student with feedback on Assessments, describing
their progression towards achievement of the CLOs and providing advice about how to best
approach their learning throughout the remainder of their Course.
Consistent with a criterion and standards referenced approach, where grades are provided, the
allocation of a grade must reflect the level of Student attainment in relation to Benchmarked
Standards. Any scaling of marks must be justifiable by reference to Benchmarked Standards
and endorsed by the Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Education).
Consensus moderation must be employed by Assessment Panels to ensure reliable judgements
in relation to Benchmarked Standards during all phases of the Assessment cycle.

the privacy of any individual who may be identifiable through any usage of personal

GenAI tools may also extract sensitive information from provided data and chat histories, and
reshare them with other users in the form of search results. Researchers should assume that
any information they enter in these tools will become public.
There are several security risks associated with the use of GenAI tools, such as exposing
personal information and manipulating it maliciously, as well as cyber and fraud attacks.

management, researchers must carefully consider their privacy and data security
responsibilities when using GenAI tools.

This policy applies to:
Complaints made by prospective, current and former Students or members of the public about
the University or University-related conduct, whether occurring in Australia or overseas; and
all persons involved in making, responding to, managing or resolving those Complaints.
Where legislation or another University or external framework provides a specific process for
dealing with all or part of a matter, the University may refer or manage that matter under the
applicable process. This includes matters concerning academic review or appeal, public
interest disclosures, misconduct, staff performance, privacy, employment or workplace
grievances, the ECU Student Guild, and third-party organisations.
This does not prevent the University from considering a distinct Complaint about its
administration of, or response to, the matter.
Where a matter engages more than one framework, the University will determine whether the
relevant issues are to be managed separately, sequentially, concurrently or in a coordinated
manner and will inform the Complainant of the applicable pathway.

4.9 Research Ethics and Integrity
All research projects undertaken at ECU must undertake appropriate risk assessment prior
to commencement. ECU has established policies and processes for the management of
risks in research, including but not limited to, the ethics review and risk management. Such
risk assessment processes are important in the identification and management of risks
associated with the use of GenAI. Researchers should ensure that they are transparent and
honest in their use or intended use of GenAI throughout these ethics and other risk
assessment processes.

documents_checked.text:
Safety and Risk
The University will comply with applicable legislation when undertaking Research, including
when partnering with other entities in joint Research projects.
Researchers must take reasonable and practicable steps to ensure they are aware of their
responsibilities with respect to the applicable Occupational Safety and Health legislation and
governing regulations, including regulatory requirements for Research involving radiation,
biosafety, and hazardous substances.
To the extent reasonable and required, the University will ensure work health and safety
advice is available to Researchers through the University’s Work Health and Safety
Management System. This will include information on work health and safety advisors, safety
and health representatives, local and University Work Health and Safety Committees, and any
other relevant committees, such as the Radiation Biosafety Hazardous Substances Committee
and Persons Conducting Business or Undertakings.

case_summary.critical_risk_criterion: Authorised, safe execution, meaningful human intervention and accountable research responsibility.
case_summary.critical_gap_explanation: N096 prohibits commencing research without completed WHS risk and REMS governance approvals, while N097 bars public GenAI from directly conducting research, requires DCS validation for GenAI tools, and holds human researchers accountable for all outputs.
case_summary.case_note: ECU prohibits unapproved autonomous research execution under N096, which bars commencing research until WHS risk and REMS governance approvals are completed, and N097, which prohibits using public GenAI in the direct conduct of research and requires DCS validation of GenAI software. Human researchers remain personally accountable for all research outputs and authorship under N097 and N096.

supporting_passages.text:
This policy applies to:
Complaints made by prospective, current and former Students or members of the public about
the University or University-related conduct, whether occurring in Australia or overseas; and
all persons involved in making, responding to, managing or resolving those Complaints.
Where legislation or another University or external framework provides a specific process for
dealing with all or part of a matter, the University may refer or manage that matter under the
applicable process. This includes matters concerning academic review or appeal, public
interest disclosures, misconduct, staff performance, privacy, employment or workplace
grievances, the ECU Student Guild, and third-party organisations.
This does not prevent the University from considering a distinct Complaint about its
administration of, or response to, the matter.
Where a matter engages more than one framework, the University will determine whether the
relevant issues are to be managed separately, sequentially, concurrently or in a coordinated
manner and will inform the Complainant of the applicable pathway.

Security 4 and De-identification 5
The University will take a proactive approach to manage Personal Information and Sensitive
Personal Information (including Health Information) by ensuring appropriate safeguards and
protocols are in place, including by:
only collecting and retaining Personal Information that is necessary for its functions and not
retaining information longer than required;
protecting against Information Breach Incidents, including from misuse, interference, loss and
from unauthorised access, modification, and disclosure;
following a ‘privacy by design’ approach for processes and system change initiatives;
where relevant, undertaking a Privacy Impact Assessment to appropriately consider and
manage privacy risks and impact;
aligning accountabilities and responsibilities of Relevant Data Owners in line with the Data
Governance Framework; and
ensuring storage and retention protocols under the Records Management Policy.
The University will take reasonable steps to de-identify or destroy Personal Information about
an individual where the:
University no longer needs the information for any purpose for which the information may be
used or disclosed by the entity under this policy;
information is not contained in a Commonwealth record; and
University is not required by or under an Australian law, a court or tribunal order, to retain the
information.

Personal Information and Sensitive Personal Information in accordance with this policy.

University will take reasonable steps to notify the individual or ensure that the individual is
aware of the collection, and that the collection is fair and reasonable in the circumstances.
The notification must contain the following and may take the form of a collection notice or
other appropriate forms of communication (including digital interfaces, system notices, or
contractual arrangements):
the University’s contact details;

collection;

Act processes;
the purpose for collecting the information, and any laws that require the particular information
to be collected (if applicable);

The University will take steps to reasonably ensure that the Personal Information it collects,
uses, or discloses is accurate, up-to-date and complete.
The University recognises that, under the PRIS Act, the Information Privacy Principle relating to
access and correction does not apply to agencies subject to the FOI Act, and that requests for
access to, and correction of, Personal Information for the University are primarily governed
under the FOI Act mechanisms.
The University may, at its discretion, provide access to Personal Information outside of the FOI
Act where it is reasonable and practicable to do so. The University may decline informal
requests where it considers it appropriate to require a formal application under the FOI Act.
Individuals may apply or request access to their own Personal Information or correction of this
Personal Information by contacting the relevant University area, or by application to the
Privacy Officer.
The University will aim to respond to informal access or correction requests within 45 days,
noting that statutory timeframes apply where requests are made under the FOI Act. If the
University determines that it is not reasonable to allow access or amend an individual’s
Personal Information, it will inform the individual of the reasons for denial of access or
correction.
Individuals may also apply under the FOI Act for an amendment of Personal Information.

Security 4 and De-identification 5
The University will take a proactive approach to manage Personal Information and Sensitive
Personal Information (including Health Information) by ensuring appropriate safeguards and
protocols are in place, including by:
only collecting and retaining Personal Information that is necessary for its functions and not
retaining information longer than required;
protecting against Information Breach Incidents, including from misuse, interference, loss and
from unauthorised access, modification, and disclosure;
following a ‘privacy by design’ approach for processes and system change initiatives;
where relevant, undertaking a Privacy Impact Assessment to appropriately consider and
manage privacy risks and impact;
aligning accountabilities and responsibilities of Relevant Data Owners in line with the Data
Governance Framework; and
ensuring storage and retention protocols under the Records Management Policy.
The University will take reasonable steps to de-identify or destroy Personal Information about
an individual where the:
University no longer needs the information for any purpose for which the information may be
used or disclosed by the entity under this policy;
information is not contained in a Commonwealth record; and
University is not required by or under an Australian law, a court or tribunal order, to retain the
information.

The University will take steps to reasonably ensure that the Personal Information it collects,
uses, or discloses is accurate, up-to-date and complete.
The University recognises that, under the PRIS Act, the Information Privacy Principle relating to
access and correction does not apply to agencies subject to the FOI Act, and that requests for
access to, and correction of, Personal Information for the University are primarily governed
under the FOI Act mechanisms.
The University may, at its discretion, provide access to Personal Information outside of the FOI
Act where it is reasonable and practicable to do so. The University may decline informal
requests where it considers it appropriate to require a formal application under the FOI Act.
Individuals may apply or request access to their own Personal Information or correction of this
Personal Information by contacting the relevant University area, or by application to the
Privacy Officer.
The University will aim to respond to informal access or correction requests within 45 days,
noting that statutory timeframes apply where requests are made under the FOI Act. If the
University determines that it is not reasonable to allow access or amend an individual’s
Personal Information, it will inform the individual of the reasons for denial of access or
correction.
Individuals may also apply under the FOI Act for an amendment of Personal Information.

documents_checked.document_title: Acceptable Use of Information Systems Policy
documents_checked.text:
The University reserves the right to decide who will and will not be provided access to
University Information Systems and to remove access should the University deem access to no
longer be required or to no longer be in the University’s best interests.
Authorised Users provided with accounts enabling access to University Information Systems
accept accounts on the understanding they are for the exclusive use of the Authorised User
and must not be shared or used by anyone other than the Authorised User.
Passwords, accounts and documented processes required for the access of University
information must be protected and secured in accordance with the conditions under which
access has been provided.
Authorised Users must not deliberately avoid or attempt to avoid authentication or conceal or
attempt to conceal their identity whilst using University information Systems.
Authorised Users must not acquire, possess, trade, or use hardware or software tools that
could be employed to evaluate or compromise Information Security.
Authorised Users who reasonably suspect the privacy and security of their account has been
compromised must immediately report their concern to the CIO or their nominee.

documents_checked.text:
The PIA will ensure privacy considerations are embedded early in the planning and operational
activities for all initiatives - projects, programs, systems, or changes in processes that:
Collect, use, store, disclose, or transfer personal information;
Introduce new or significantly changed ways of handling personal information;
Are likely to have a high rated privacy risk or significant impact on individuals’ privacy.
Step 1 – Privacy Threshold Assessment
For every initiative involving new or changed ways of handling personal information, the
Project Officer or Manager must conduct a Privacy Threshold Assessment (PTA).
The PTA is in the format of a short questionnaire to triage if further detailed Privacy Impact
Assessment is required.
Depending on the outcome of the PTA, some assessments will end at this point. Some will
proceed to Step 2 Conduct a PIA.
Step 2 – Conduct a Privacy Impact Assessment
The PIA is comprised of a number of questions to guide Staff through a systematic assessment
of the initiative.
The Project Officer or Manager are responsible for initiating and completing the PIA.
The PIA must be approved by the Project Sponsor.
The PIA must be submitted to Privacy team (Privacy@ECU).
The Privacy Officer or delegate will assess the PIA.

Automated Decision-Making 7
The University is committed to ensuring transparency, fairness and accountability in all
automated decision-making processes including by:
assessment of the impact of the automated decision-making processes;
regular review to minimise bias and ensure compliance with applicable privacy laws; and
taking reasonable steps to notify individuals of use of automated decision-making processes.
The University, during its functions and activities, may:
use computer programs, including rule-based systems and artificial intelligence or machine
learning technologies; and
use or engage in third-party services that use computer programs, including rule-based
systems and artificial intelligence or machine learning technologies,
to assist or support in the review and decision-making which could significantly affect
individual rights or interests.
Where these decisions relate to eligibility for services, access to benefits, or other outcomes
that may significantly affect an individual, the University will take reasonable steps to notify
individuals of the:
types of Personal Information used;
nature of decisions made; and
human intervention and review controls in place.
Individuals may request human review of decisions that significantly affect them where
automated decision-making has been used.

This policy applies to:
Complaints made by prospective, current and former Students or members of the public about
the University or University-related conduct, whether occurring in Australia or overseas; and
all persons involved in making, responding to, managing or resolving those Complaints.
Where legislation or another University or external framework provides a specific process for
dealing with all or part of a matter, the University may refer or manage that matter under the
applicable process. This includes matters concerning academic review or appeal, public
interest disclosures, misconduct, staff performance, privacy, employment or workplace
grievances, the ECU Student Guild, and third-party organisations.
This does not prevent the University from considering a distinct Complaint about its
administration of, or response to, the matter.
Where a matter engages more than one framework, the University will determine whether the
relevant issues are to be managed separately, sequentially, concurrently or in a coordinated
manner and will inform the Complainant of the applicable pathway.

longer be required or to no longer be in the University’s best interests.
Authorised Users provided with accounts enabling access to University Information Systems
accept accounts on the understanding they are for the exclusive use of the Authorised User
and must not be shared or used by anyone other than the Authorised User.
Passwords, accounts and documented processes required for the access of University
information must be protected and secured in accordance with the conditions under which
access has been provided.
Authorised Users must not deliberately avoid or attempt to avoid authentication or conceal or
attempt to conceal their identity whilst using University information Systems.
Authorised Users must not acquire, possess, trade, or use hardware or software tools that
could be employed to evaluate or compromise Information Security.
Authorised Users who reasonably suspect the privacy and security of their account has been
compromised must immediately report their concern to the CIO or their nominee.

Automated Decision-Making 7
The University is committed to ensuring transparency, fairness and accountability in all
automated decision-making processes including by:
assessment of the impact of the automated decision-making processes;
regular review to minimise bias and ensure compliance with applicable privacy laws; and
taking reasonable steps to notify individuals of use of automated decision-making processes.
The University, during its functions and activities, may:
use computer programs, including rule-based systems and artificial intelligence or machine
learning technologies; and
use or engage in third-party services that use computer programs, including rule-based
systems and artificial intelligence or machine learning technologies,
to assist or support in the review and decision-making which could significantly affect
individual rights or interests.
Where these decisions relate to eligibility for services, access to benefits, or other outcomes
that may significantly affect an individual, the University will take reasonable steps to notify
individuals of the:
types of Personal Information used;
nature of decisions made; and
human intervention and review controls in place.
Individuals may request human review of decisions that significantly affect them where
automated decision-making has been used.

The PIA will ensure privacy considerations are embedded early in the planning and operational
activities for all initiatives - projects, programs, systems, or changes in processes that:
Collect, use, store, disclose, or transfer personal information;
Introduce new or significantly changed ways of handling personal information;
Are likely to have a high rated privacy risk or significant impact on individuals’ privacy.
Step 1 – Privacy Threshold Assessment
For every initiative involving new or changed ways of handling personal information, the
Project Officer or Manager must conduct a Privacy Threshold Assessment (PTA).
The PTA is in the format of a short questionnaire to triage if further detailed Privacy Impact
Assessment is required.
Depending on the outcome of the PTA, some assessments will end at this point. Some will
proceed to Step 2 Conduct a PIA.
Step 2 – Conduct a Privacy Impact Assessment
The PIA is comprised of a number of questions to guide Staff through a systematic assessment
of the initiative.
The Project Officer or Manager are responsible for initiating and completing the PIA.
The PIA must be approved by the Project Sponsor.
The PIA must be submitted to Privacy team (Privacy@ECU).
The Privacy Officer or delegate will assess the PIA.

This policy applies to:
Complaints made by prospective, current and former Students or members of the public about
the University or University-related conduct, whether occurring in Australia or overseas; and
all persons involved in making, responding to, managing or resolving those Complaints.
Where legislation or another University or external framework provides a specific process for
dealing with all or part of a matter, the University may refer or manage that matter under the
applicable process. This includes matters concerning academic review or appeal, public
interest disclosures, misconduct, staff performance, privacy, employment or workplace
grievances, the ECU Student Guild, and third-party organisations.
This does not prevent the University from considering a distinct Complaint about its
administration of, or response to, the matter.
Where a matter engages more than one framework, the University will determine whether the
relevant issues are to be managed separately, sequentially, concurrently or in a coordinated
manner and will inform the Complainant of the applicable pathway.

case_summary.critical_risk_criterion: Verifiable authority before binding academic representation and before disclosure of confidential student information.
case_summary.critical_gap_explanation: Although general protections in N088 (7.3), N077 (1.6), and N083 (5.1-5.2) bar third-party appeals, password sharing, and unauthorised personal data disclosure, no relevant verification mechanism was identified in the documents and searches checked for staff to confirm authority before binding representation or confidential disclosure when an AI agent uses a student's delegated SSO/email account.
case_summary.case_note: Murdoch's Student Appeals Procedure (N088, 7.3) prohibits another person from making an appeal on a student's behalf, while IT Conditions of Use (N077, 1.6) prohibits password sharing and Privacy Policy (N083) restricts personal information disclosure. However, no relevant verification boundary was identified in the documents and searches checked to prevent an AI agent using delegated SSO credentials from binding academic representation or receiving confidential student data in routine staff correspondence, leaving a critical gap.

case_summary.critical_risk_criterion: Attributable human/group responsibility and traceable disclosure of relevant AI assistance. Access differences become critical where a required tool blocks participation without a workable alternative.
case_summary.critical_gap_explanation: While N087 (2.1, 6.3.1) requires collective honesty in groupwork and authorisation for AI-produced work, Murdoch policies lack an operational mechanism for attributable human/group responsibility and traceable disclosure of individual AI assistance across group members.
case_summary.case_note: Murdoch's Student Academic Integrity Policy (N087) requires collective honesty in groupwork (2.1) and prohibits submitting AI-produced work without assessment authorisation (6.3.1), while N112 defers unit-level GenAI expectations to Unit Outlines. No relevant provision was identified in the documents and searches checked requiring group-level tracking or traceable disclosure of individual AI assistance or addressing unequal AI tool access, leaving a critical gap.

case_summary.critical_risk_criterion: Authorised, safe execution, meaningful human intervention and accountable research responsibility.
case_summary.critical_gap_explanation: While N179, N077, N080, and N172 provide general IT access, incident-management, and research-conduct rules, no relevant provision was identified in the documents and searches checked establishing authorisation, safety boundaries, meaningful human intervention, or accountable PI responsibility for an autonomous multi-agent AI system executing connected laboratory or computational actions without step-level human review.
case_summary.case_note: Murdoch's ICT Security Policy (N179), Information Security Incident Management Policy (N080), and the hosted Australian Code (N172) establish general IT access controls, incident escalation, and research-conduct principles. However, no relevant provision was identified in the documents and searches checked governing autonomous multi-agent AI systems executing connected laboratory or computational research without human verification, leaving a critical gap.

6. Automated Decision-Making
6.1 The University may use automated systems or tools to assist in decision
making processes. These may include analysing personal information to
support administrative, educational, research, or service-related functions.

outcome; and

prevent unlawful discrimination, bias, or adverse impacts arising
from automated processes.

5.4 Contract cheating

student misconduct.

cheating, the course coordinator will refer it to the Academic Integrity Officer for
investigation to decide if it can be substantiated.

they will notify the course coordinator who will report the matter to the appropriate
head of school or director. (refer to clause 5.2.2 of this procedure)

Integrity Officer will also notify the Pro Vice Chancellor, Education and the

5.4.4 If the Academic Integrity Officer decides that contract cheating cannot be
substantiated, they will notify the course coordinator and provide the reason for their
decision.

6.6.1.1 The University of Notre Dame Australia owns the copyright in materials
presented in classes. Accordingly:
• Students may only use the materials presented in classes, and any recording
of a class, for their personal study.
• Use of these materials or recording for any other purpose, or distribution or
sharing of this material without the University’s express permission will
infringe the University’s copyright.
• Students are not permitted to record these materials on personal devices
without first obtaining permission from the staff member teaching the class.

4.5 Making a Complaint About the University’s Handling of Personal Information
4.5.1 If an individual wishes to make a complaint about the University’s handling of personal
information he or she should contact the Legal Office of the relevant Campus. The
Legal Office will try to resolve the matter informally.
4.5.2 If a complaint cannot be resolved, the individual will be required to formally lodge the
complaint in writing to the Legal Office with any supporting documentation attached to
the complaint.
4.5.3 The University will deal with the complaint within 30 business days and advise the
individual lodging the complaint of the outcome.
4.5.4 If the individual is unhappy with the outcome he or she may refer the complaint to the
Office of the Australian Information Commissioner. Further information about the
external dispute resolution can be found at www.oaic.gov.au.

case_summary.case_note: Procedure: Assessment and Examinations (N026, 6.2.1) requires group assessments to identify individual contributions and resolve group issues, while N028 (4.5.2.3) conditions generative AI use on express authorisation. Although paid AI access disparities within groups are not explicitly regulated, the existing rules establish structured discretion without a critical gap.

out in section 6.5 of this policy.

further internal appeal.

Tier 2 – AI assistance
If your assessment is assigned Tier 2, you may use AI tools only for the specific
purposes explicitly permitted by your unit coordinator. Don’t assume that AI use
is allowed beyond what is stated in your assessment instructions. Tier 2 does not
mean ‘general permission to use AI.’

assessment must be your own work, and you remain responsible for all content
submitted, including work that has been shaped or edited using AI tools.

evidence.text:
6.9 Improper use of Artificial Intelligence tools
(a) The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is permitted only as an educational/study tool to assist
students in their research and writing to be used in accordance with 6.8(b), and not as a
replacement of their critical thinking and analysis.
(b) Where any AI-generated outputs are used in assessments;
i. they must be appropriately acknowledged for the submission, including a formal
reference, along with any other sources used;
ii. there must be a clear indication of where in an assignment AI-generated material is
used;
iii. it is the responsibility of the student to check the accuracy of all information generated
by AI study tools;
(c) Improper use of AI-generated outputs in any assessment item/task may lead to the occurrence of
academic misconduct referred to in this policy and a penalty or penalties for a proven incident or
incidents of academic misconduct may be imposed in accordance with the relevant penalty matrix.
(d) Unit Coordinators may use AI tools in an assessment within a unit, subject to clearly publishing
the intent and the limitations of the use of such tools within the unit outline.

6.9 Improper use of Artificial Intelligence tools
(a) The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is permitted only as an educational/study tool to assist
students in their research and writing to be used in accordance with 6.8(b), and not as a
replacement of their critical thinking and analysis.
(b) Where any AI-generated outputs are used in assessments;
i. they must be appropriately acknowledged for the submission, including a formal
reference, along with any other sources used;
ii. there must be a clear indication of where in an assignment AI-generated material is
used;
iii. it is the responsibility of the student to check the accuracy of all information generated
by AI study tools;
(c) Improper use of AI-generated outputs in any assessment item/task may lead to the occurrence of
academic misconduct referred to in this policy and a penalty or penalties for a proven incident or
incidents of academic misconduct may be imposed in accordance with the relevant penalty matrix.
(d) Unit Coordinators may use AI tools in an assessment within a unit, subject to clearly publishing
the intent and the limitations of the use of such tools within the unit outline.

Tier 2 – AI assistance
If your assessment is assigned Tier 2, you may use AI tools only for the specific
purposes explicitly permitted by your unit coordinator. Don’t assume that AI use
is allowed beyond what is stated in your assessment instructions. Tier 2 does not
mean ‘general permission to use AI.’

assessment must be your own work, and you remain responsible for all content
submitted, including work that has been shaped or edited using AI tools.

processing tools that only consider spelling or grammar errors.

can circumvent the need for students to develop their own skills and can mask their true level of
expertise. The University, therefore, does not permit students to use paid or unpaid editorial
assistance, including artificial intelligence/translation/automated writing tools, except in limited
authorised circumstances, as set out in sub-clause 6.8(b).

Breach Policy.

monitoring outcomes, including results of reviews, audits, incidents, breaches, reported concerns,
and changes to legal or regulatory obligations.

(a) The University will investigate and take seriously complaints made by individuals relating to the

include sufficient details of the Personal Information concerned, and the conduct alleged to be
inconsistent with this Policy or constitutes an interference with privacy.

as practical but where possible within 45 University working days.

1 Purpose
1.1 This policy provides for students to request a review of an academic decision relating to them, and to
appeal if they are dissatisfied with the outcomes of that review. The policy sets out the student’s right
review and to appeal the results of any review to the Appeals Committee of the Academic Board.
1.2 This policy applies in all instances where a student is seeking a review of an academic decision unless
another review process is prescribed in a specific statute, regulation, rule or policy pertaining to the
matter in question.

(a) The University will investigate and take seriously complaints made by individuals relating to the
University’s handling and management of Personal Information, including disclosure of their
information, where that is contrary to this Policy, or an interference with their privacy in accordance
with the PRIS Act.
(b) Complaints must be submitted in writing to the UWA Privacy Office (privacy@uwa.edu.au) and
include sufficient details of the Personal Information concerned, and the conduct alleged to be
inconsistent with this Policy or constitutes an interference with privacy.

as practical but where possible within 45 University working days.

4.5 Monitoring and Continual Improvement
(a) A Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) to identify privacy risks and measures to mitigate them must
be undertaken by the University where a new process or system involving personal information is
implemented or existing process changed that could reasonably have a significant impact on the
privacy of individuals.
(b) The University monitors, measures, analyses and evaluates information privacy compliance
performance, controls and processes to ensure they are and remain appropriate and effective.
(c) Significant risks, compliance matters and breaches are reported to relevant University committees
and external supervisory agencies where required in accordance with the University’s Information
Breach Policy.
(d) The University must continuously improve its information privacy practices in response to
monitoring outcomes, including results of reviews, audits, incidents, breaches, reported concerns,
and changes to legal or regulatory obligations.

documents_checked.text:
6.9 Improper use of Artificial Intelligence tools
(a) The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is permitted only as an educational/study tool to assist
students in their research and writing to be used in accordance with 6.8(b), and not as a
replacement of their critical thinking and analysis.
(b) Where any AI-generated outputs are used in assessments;
i. they must be appropriately acknowledged for the submission, including a formal
reference, along with any other sources used;
ii. there must be a clear indication of where in an assignment AI-generated material is
used;
iii. it is the responsibility of the student to check the accuracy of all information generated
by AI study tools;
(c) Improper use of AI-generated outputs in any assessment item/task may lead to the occurrence of
academic misconduct referred to in this policy and a penalty or penalties for a proven incident or
incidents of academic misconduct may be imposed in accordance with the relevant penalty matrix.
(d) Unit Coordinators may use AI tools in an assessment within a unit, subject to clearly publishing
the intent and the limitations of the use of such tools within the unit outline.

• a statement defining expected contributions from each team member may be required to

6.9 Improper use of Artificial Intelligence tools
(a) The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is permitted only as an educational/study tool to assist
students in their research and writing to be used in accordance with 6.8(b), and not as a
replacement of their critical thinking and analysis.
(b) Where any AI-generated outputs are used in assessments;
i. they must be appropriately acknowledged for the submission, including a formal
reference, along with any other sources used;
ii. there must be a clear indication of where in an assignment AI-generated material is
used;
iii. it is the responsibility of the student to check the accuracy of all information generated
by AI study tools;
(c) Improper use of AI-generated outputs in any assessment item/task may lead to the occurrence of
academic misconduct referred to in this policy and a penalty or penalties for a proven incident or
incidents of academic misconduct may be imposed in accordance with the relevant penalty matrix.
(d) Unit Coordinators may use AI tools in an assessment within a unit, subject to clearly publishing
the intent and the limitations of the use of such tools within the unit outline.

documents_checked.text:
Tier 2 – AI assistance
If your assessment is assigned Tier 2, you may use AI tools only for the specific
purposes explicitly permitted by your unit coordinator. Don’t assume that AI use
is allowed beyond what is stated in your assessment instructions. Tier 2 does not
mean ‘general permission to use AI.’
In Tier 2 assessments, AI tools may be used before or after your own work, but not
as a substitute for your thinking, analysis, or writing. The majority of the
assessment must be your own work, and you remain responsible for all content
submitted, including work that has been shaped or edited using AI tools.

appeal if they are dissatisfied with the outcomes of that review. The policy sets out the student’s right
review and to appeal the results of any review to the Appeals Committee of the Academic Board.

another review process is prescribed in a specific statute, regulation, rule or policy pertaining to the
matter in question.

6.9 Improper use of Artificial Intelligence tools
(a) The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is permitted only as an educational/study tool to assist
students in their research and writing to be used in accordance with 6.8(b), and not as a
replacement of their critical thinking and analysis.
(b) Where any AI-generated outputs are used in assessments;
i. they must be appropriately acknowledged for the submission, including a formal
reference, along with any other sources used;
ii. there must be a clear indication of where in an assignment AI-generated material is
used;
iii. it is the responsibility of the student to check the accuracy of all information generated
by AI study tools;
(c) Improper use of AI-generated outputs in any assessment item/task may lead to the occurrence of
academic misconduct referred to in this policy and a penalty or penalties for a proven incident or
incidents of academic misconduct may be imposed in accordance with the relevant penalty matrix.
(d) Unit Coordinators may use AI tools in an assessment within a unit, subject to clearly publishing
the intent and the limitations of the use of such tools within the unit outline.

case_summary.critical_gap_explanation: Under Protocol v1.1 (adopted after preliminary review on 2026-11-15), while N044 and N128 cover authorised AI contributions and human group responsibility, no relevant provision was identified in the documents and searches checked establishing an operational consent, authorisation, and data-retention boundary for a persistent-memory AI agent ingesting group members' personal information in a shared workspace.
case_summary.case_note: UWA policies N044 and N128 regulate attributable AI contributions and human group accountability, while N071 and N067 govern automated agents and personal information. However, UWA lacks operational rules for group-member consent, workspace authorisation, and cross-session memory retention when an AI agent joins a shared student workspace, leaving a critical gap.

documents_checked.text:
6.9 Improper use of Artificial Intelligence tools
(a) The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is permitted only as an educational/study tool to assist
students in their research and writing to be used in accordance with 6.8(b), and not as a
replacement of their critical thinking and analysis.
(b) Where any AI-generated outputs are used in assessments;
i. they must be appropriately acknowledged for the submission, including a formal
reference, along with any other sources used;
ii. there must be a clear indication of where in an assignment AI-generated material is
used;
iii. it is the responsibility of the student to check the accuracy of all information generated
by AI study tools;
(c) Improper use of AI-generated outputs in any assessment item/task may lead to the occurrence of
academic misconduct referred to in this policy and a penalty or penalties for a proven incident or
incidents of academic misconduct may be imposed in accordance with the relevant penalty matrix.
(d) Unit Coordinators may use AI tools in an assessment within a unit, subject to clearly publishing
the intent and the limitations of the use of such tools within the unit outline.

AI tools can help you find sources and references and sort through a lot of
content quickly. But they can sometimes invent sources or details. This is
sometimes called ‘hallucination.’ They can also misunderstand what a source
concludes. Because of this, you still need to check that each source is real and
reliable.
AI tools also have limits when comparing sources and making judgements about
them. You still need to read and analyse each source yourself. This helps you
check that the summaries and claims are accurate. It also helps you make
connections between sources.

documents_checked.document_title: Academic Integrity Policy and Schedules (pdf, 423 KB)
documents_checked.text:
6.9 Improper use of Artificial Intelligence tools
(a) The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is permitted only as an educational/study tool to assist
students in their research and writing to be used in accordance with 6.8(b), and not as a
replacement of their critical thinking and analysis.
(b) Where any AI-generated outputs are used in assessments;
i. they must be appropriately acknowledged for the submission, including a formal
reference, along with any other sources used;
ii. there must be a clear indication of where in an assignment AI-generated material is
used;
iii. it is the responsibility of the student to check the accuracy of all information generated
by AI study tools;
(c) Improper use of AI-generated outputs in any assessment item/task may lead to the occurrence of
academic misconduct referred to in this policy and a penalty or penalties for a proven incident or
incidents of academic misconduct may be imposed in accordance with the relevant penalty matrix.
(d) Unit Coordinators may use AI tools in an assessment within a unit, subject to clearly publishing
the intent and the limitations of the use of such tools within the unit outline.

case_summary.critical_risk_criterion: Human verification of citations and claims, accurate attribution and protection of confidential research information.
case_summary.critical_gap_explanation: Under Protocol v1.1 (adopted after preliminary review on 2026-11-15), N128, N044 6.5(d)(vi)/6.9(b), and N055 8(B)(8)/9/17(C) enforce human verification of citations and claims, accurate attribution, and protection of confidential research material.
case_summary.case_note: UWA Student Guide N128 and Academic Integrity Policy N044 require verifying AI-retrieved sources and disclosing AI use, while Research Integrity Policy N055 enforces authorship accountability, data confidentiality, and bans on fabricated citations. Staff-specific AI research procedures are less explicit than student rules, though existing research-integrity and confidentiality duties address the critical risks.

(a) Individuals have the right to access Personal Information held about them by the University and to
request correction of that information where it is inaccurate, incomplete or out-of-date.

University function responsible for that information such as Student Central (for students) or People

(c) The University must take reasonable steps to provide access to, and correct, Personal Information

(d) Where the University refuses access to, or correction of, Personal Information, it must provide
reasons for the decision and information about available avenues for review or complaint.

documents_checked.text:
4.5 Monitoring and Continual Improvement
(a) A Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) to identify privacy risks and measures to mitigate them must
be undertaken by the University where a new process or system involving personal information is
implemented or existing process changed that could reasonably have a significant impact on the
privacy of individuals.
(b) The University monitors, measures, analyses and evaluates information privacy compliance
performance, controls and processes to ensure they are and remain appropriate and effective.
(c) Significant risks, compliance matters and breaches are reported to relevant University committees
and external supervisory agencies where required in accordance with the University’s Information
Breach Policy.
(d) The University must continuously improve its information privacy practices in response to
monitoring outcomes, including results of reviews, audits, incidents, breaches, reported concerns,
and changes to legal or regulatory obligations.

(a) A Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) to identify privacy risks and measures to mitigate them must
be undertaken by the University where a new process or system involving personal information is
implemented or existing process changed that could reasonably have a significant impact on the
privacy of individuals.

performance, controls and processes to ensure they are and remain appropriate and effective.

and external supervisory agencies where required in accordance with the University’s Information
Breach Policy.
(d) The University must continuously improve its information privacy practices in response to
monitoring outcomes, including results of reviews, audits, incidents, breaches, reported concerns,
and changes to legal or regulatory obligations.

documents_checked.text:
4.5 Monitoring and Continual Improvement
(a) A Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) to identify privacy risks and measures to mitigate them must
be undertaken by the University where a new process or system involving personal information is
implemented or existing process changed that could reasonably have a significant impact on the
privacy of individuals.
(b) The University monitors, measures, analyses and evaluates information privacy compliance
performance, controls and processes to ensure they are and remain appropriate and effective.
(c) Significant risks, compliance matters and breaches are reported to relevant University committees
and external supervisory agencies where required in accordance with the University’s Information
Breach Policy.
(d) The University must continuously improve its information privacy practices in response to
monitoring outcomes, including results of reviews, audits, incidents, breaches, reported concerns,
and changes to legal or regulatory obligations.

case_summary.critical_risk_criterion: Purpose-bounded authorisation for combined standing powers, with security, intervention and contestability of consequential actions.
case_summary.critical_gap_explanation: Under Protocol v1.1 (adopted after preliminary review on 2026-11-15), while N071 and N072 provide least-privilege security and CIO suspension powers, no relevant provision was identified in the documents and searches checked establishing a unified purpose-bounded authorisation and per-action contestability framework for an AI agent exercising combined standing powers across LMS, enrolment, advising, and assessment systems.
case_summary.case_note: UWA Acceptable Use of IT Policy N071 enforces least-privilege access and bans credential sharing for automated agents, while Cyber Security Policy N072 empowers the CIO to suspend risky Digital Resource operations. However, no relevant provision was identified in the documents and searches checked establishing a unified purpose-bounded authorisation and per-action contestability framework for standing AI powers spanning LMS, enrolment, advising, and assessment systems, leaving a critical gap.
